_comment: Cross-implementation vectors for the canonical claim construction (spec §13.1).
leaf = H( 0x00 || pool || len(address) || address || identity_hash || amount_be32 )
node = H( 0x01 || min(a,b) || max(a,b) )
H is sha256 on Soroban and on Aptos, and keccak256 on EVM, so digests are
per chain by design - what is identical across chains is the construction
rule, not the bytes. These values are the sha256 ones.
The identical vectors are asserted from the contract side, in
Stellar-Contracts/contracts/grainhack-escrow/src/test.rs. The two copies must
stay byte-identical. If one side changes, its own test goes red first.
History worth keeping: these two implementations drifted before this vector
existed. The contract hashed pool, XDR address, identity and a 16-byte
amount; the backend hashed identity, UTF-8 address, an 8-byte amount, chain
id and event id. A root built by the backend could not be claimed against
the contract. Neither construction was correct - the contract's XDR address
forced Stellar encoding into chain-agnostic code, and the backend had no
pool binding, an int64 that wrapped on negatives, and unprefixed
variable-length fields that collided. Both were replaced by the above.
chain_id and event_id are deliberately absent. One escrow is one event on
one chain and the root lives inside that contract, so a leaf has nowhere
else to be replayed. Do not re-add them.
construction: H(0x00 || pool_u8 || addr_len_u16_be || address || identity_hash_32 || amount_be32)

_comment: The same construction with Aptos's address encoding.
leaf = sha256(0x00 || pool_u8 || 0x0020 || address_32 || identity_hash_32 || amount_be32)
WHY THE ADDRESS IS RAW BYTES HERE AND A STRING ON SOROBAN.
A Stellar strkey has exactly one valid spelling, so hashing the canonical
string is safe. An Aptos address does not: 0x1, 0x01 and the 64-digit
padded form all denote the same account. Hashing a string would make the
leaf depend on how the address happened to be written when it was
registered, and a claim against a mis-spelled leaf fails permanently
against a root that cannot be corrected. So on Aptos the field is the 32
raw bytes, with its true length prefix of 32.
The construction RULE is unchanged - that is the point. Each chain uses its
own address encoding inside one shared field order.
NO GO CHANGE WAS NEEDED TO PRODUCE THIS.
ClaimLeaf.Hash writes uint16(len(addr)) then addr, where addr is
[]byte(ClaimAddress). Setting ClaimAddress to the 32 raw bytes therefore
emits exactly the Aptos encoding through the production builder, so this
vector is generated by the code that will build a real root rather than by
a second implementation written to match it.
Asserted from the Move side in aptos-contracts, test
`the_leaf_matches_the_pinned_cross_implementation_vector`. Three mutations
survived before this existed - the leaf prefix, the pool byte, and the
amount's left padding could all be changed with every Move test still
passing, because nothing external pinned the digest.
aptos_leaf_vector.construction: sha256(0x00 || pool_u8 || addr_len_u16_be || address_32 || identity_hash_32 || amount_be32)

_comment: WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS.
The leaf was pinned across implementations; the TREE was not. Every
internal-node rule - the 0x01 prefix, the ascending leaf sort, promoting
an odd node rather than duplicating it - was free to differ between the
backend and a verifier while every test on both sides stayed green. The
first symptom would have been a real contributor unable to claim against
a root that cannot be corrected.
Measured, not asserted: with nodePrefix deleted, and with the leaf sort
reversed, the entire Go suite still passed before these vectors existed.
WHAT IS PINNED.
Three rules, all of which change a root here if they change anywhere:
1. Leaves are sorted ASCENDING by digest before the tree is built, so
the same set always yields the same root regardless of query order.
2. An internal node is H(0x01 || min(a,b) || max(a,b)). The prefix is
what stops a crafted internal node being presented as a leaf; the
sort is what removes left/right position from each proof step.
3. An odd node at any level is PROMOTED unchanged to the next level,
never duplicated. Duplicating is the CVE-2012-2459 shape, where two
different leaf sets produce one root.
LEAF COUNTS, AND WHY THESE ONES.
Because sibling pairs are sorted inside the node hash, reversing the leaf
sort is INVISIBLE at power-of-two counts and changes the root at every
other count. Measured:
n=2 identical   n=3 DIFFERENT   n=4 identical   n=5 DIFFERENT
n=6 DIFFERENT   n=7 DIFFERENT   n=8 identical
So 3, 5, 6 and 7 are here specifically because they are the counts that
can catch it, and 1 and 2 anchor the degenerate cases. 38 is the real
founding contributor pool size (37 members plus the one backfilled by
migration 000071) - the first tree we intend to publish for real, and
not a power of two.
INPUT DIGESTS.
Synthetic, so the vectors pin the tree rule alone and stay valid for any
chain regardless of its address encoding. The leaf construction itself is
pinned separately above.
leaf_i = sha256( 0xFF || uint16_be(i) )   for i = 0 .. n-1
0xFF is neither the leaf prefix (0x00) nor the node prefix (0x01), so a
synthetic digest can never collide with a real leaf.
**Feed these to the tree builder in i-order, NOT pre-sorted.** Sorting is
one of the three rules under test; handing the builder a sorted list
would leave it untested.
tree_vectors.leaf_generator: leaf_i = sha256(0xFF || uint16_be(i)), i from 0, fed to the builder in i-order

_comment: One pinned proof, so the sibling path itself is cross-checked and not
merely the root. n=7 is the deepest odd tree here, so this path crosses
a promoted node - the case a duplicating implementation gets wrong.
The leaf is the FIRST in sorted order, which is leaf_i i=3 in generator
order. Verification folds each sibling in with the node rule and must
arrive at roots["7"].
